item.text:
## 2B.10 Research Note: Kishida in 2024

Net assessment: **slightly more peaceful, stable, and lawful overall, but only modestly so and within very hard external constraints**. Kishida left behind stronger rules-based coordination on Ukraine, Gaza, North Korea, and AI/cyber governance, plus tighter Japan-South Korea / Japan-NATO / G7 alignment. The counterweight is a deeper deterrence posture, sharper bloc competition, and unresolved regional tensions with China, Russia, and North Korea.

### Supports
- **[Policy Speech by Prime Minister KISHIDA Fumio to the 213th Session of the Diet](https://japan.kantei.go.jp/101_kishida/statement/202401/30shiseihoshin.html)** | Prime Minister’s Office of Japan | January 30, 2024  
  Kishida framed Japan’s foreign and security policy around the G7 Hiroshima Vision, the rule of law, and summit diplomacy, while explicitly saying Japan would pursue a peace treaty with Russia, high-level talks with North Korea, and broader cooperation with the Global South. This is a strong “lawful order” signal rather than a war-mobilization message.  
  Question IDs: `2B.10`, `2B.1`, `2B.3`, `1B.4`

- **[Summit on Peace in Ukraine (Summary)](https://japan.kantei.go.jp/101_kishida/diplomatic/202406/15ukraine.html)** | Prime Minister’s Office of Japan | June 15, 2024  
  Kishida backed a “just and lasting peace” grounded in the UN Charter and international law, and said Japan would contribute to nuclear safety, electricity, and mine action. This is clear evidence that he pushed the Ukraine file toward a more lawful and reconstruction-oriented track.  
  Question IDs: `2B.10`, `2B.4`, `2B.7`, `1B.9`

- **[G7 Leaders’ statement on Gaza](https://www.mofa.go.jp/ecm/ec/pageite_000001_00384.html)** | Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Japan | June 4, 2024  
  Japan joined a statement calling for hostage release, humanitarian aid, protection of civilians, compliance with international humanitarian law, and de-escalation. That improved the lawfulness and stability of Japan’s regional diplomacy on the Middle East crisis.  
  Question IDs: `2B.10`, `2B.4`, `2B.7`

- **[On the Current Situation Surrounding the Gaza Strip](https://www.mofa.go.jp/press/release/pressite_000001_00630.html)** | Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Japan | October 7, 2024  
  Japan urged a ceasefire, humanitarian access, and compliance with international humanitarian law while supporting U.S., Egypt, and Qatar mediation. This is direct evidence of a settlement-oriented posture that favors stability over escalation.  
  Question IDs: `2B.10`, `2B.4`, `2B.7`

- **[The Ninth Japan-China-ROK Trilateral Summit (Summary)](https://japan.kantei.go.jp/101_kishida/diplomatic/202405/27chnrok.html)** | Prime Minister’s Office of Japan | May 27, 2024  
  Kishida emphasized rule-based cooperation and urged North Korea to abandon its nuclear and ballistic missile programs, while also stressing regional economic cooperation. That is a stable, institutional approach to an inherited security crisis.  
  Question IDs: `2B.10`, `2B.1`, `1B.6`, `1B.8`

- **[Address by Prime Minister KISHIDA Fumio at the High-Level Launch Meeting of the Friends of a Fissile Material Cut-off Treaty (FMCT)](https://japan.kantei.go.jp/101_kishida/statement/202409/23fmct.html)** | Prime Minister’s Office of Japan | September 23, 2024  
  Kishida launched the FMCT Friends framework as a capstone to his disarmament diplomacy. That strengthens the lawfulness and predictability of the broader strategic environment, even if it did not by itself resolve the underlying rivalry.  
  Question IDs: `2B.10`, `1B.4`, `1B.6`, `1B.7`

- **[Kishida’s legacy: Scandals and compromise at home, global respect for security and diplomacy](https://apnews.com/article/05926b50f4f5a83a631f779d906cf06d)** | Associated Press | September 30, 2024  
  AP reported that Kishida improved ties with South Korea, deepened cooperation with the United States and other partners, and helped stabilize Japan’s regional and global reputation. It also noted criticism that he compromised with conservatives and leaned into deterrence, so this is supportive but mixed.  
  Question IDs: `2B.10`, `2B.3`, `1B.4`, `1B.8`

### Limits
- **[Address by Prime Minister at a Joint Meeting of the United States Congress](https://japan.kantei.go.jp/101_kishida/statement/202404/11speech.html)** | Prime Minister’s Office of Japan | April 11, 2024  
  Kishida emphasized counterstrike capability, defense spending, cybersecurity, and stronger U.S. extended deterrence, alongside sanctions on Russia and support for Ukraine. This helped stabilize alliances, but it also hardened bloc competition rather than making the region uniformly more peaceful.  
  Question IDs: `2B.10`, `1B.4`, `1B.8`, `1B.9`

- **[Nobel prize for A-bomb survivors' group boosts hope for Japanese seeking a nuke-free world](https://apnews.com/article/808038ef664be2f200306d5e60b76711)** | Associated Press | October 11, 2024  
  AP reported criticism that Kishida kept relying on the U.S. nuclear umbrella and did not sign the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons. That undercuts a fully peaceful/lawful reading, even if it does not erase the gains in diplomacy and de-escalation.  
  Question IDs: `2B.10`, `1B.4`, `1B.6`

### Bottom Line
- Kishida’s 2024 record is best read as **net modestly positive** on regional/international peace, stability, and lawfulness.
- The gains came mainly through **Ukraine diplomacy, Gaza ceasefire language, North Korea containment, and disarmament/nonproliferation institutions**.
- The main constraint is that he simultaneously **deepened deterrence and alliance hardening**, so the result is **more lawful and somewhat more stable than inherited, but not meaningfully demilitarized**.
